Bubble Sort

Time Complexity: O(n²)
Space Complexity: O(1)

Bubble Sort is a simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. The pass through the list is repeated until the list is sorted.

How it works:
1. Compare adjacent elements
2. Swap if they are in wrong order
3. Repeat for all elements
4. After each pass, the largest element "bubbles up" to its correct position

Best Case: O(n) - when array is already sorted
Worst Case: O(n²) - when array is reverse sorted
Average Case: O(n²)

Stable: Yes
In-place: Yes

Insertion Sort

Time Complexity: O(n²)
Space Complexity: O(1)

Insertion Sort builds the final sorted array one item at a time. It is much less efficient on large lists than more advanced algorithms such as quicksort, heapsort, or merge sort.

How it works:
1. Start with second element (assume first is sorted)
2. Compare key element with elements in sorted portion
3. Shift all larger elements one position right
4. Insert key at correct position
5. Repeat for all elements

Best Case: O(n) - when array is already sorted
Worst Case: O(n²) - when array is reverse sorted
Average Case: O(n²)

Stable: Yes
In-place: Yes
Good for: Small datasets or nearly sorted data

Selection Sort

Time Complexity: O(n²)
Space Complexity: O(1)

Selection Sort divides the input list into two parts: a sorted portion at the left end and an unsorted portion at the right end. Initially, the sorted portion is empty and the unsorted portion is the entire list.

How it works:
1. Find the minimum element in unsorted portion
2. Swap it with the first unsorted element
3. Move boundary between sorted and unsorted portions one element to the right
4. Repeat until entire array is sorted

Best Case: O(n²)
Worst Case: O(n²)
Average Case: O(n²)

Stable: No (typical implementation)
In-place: Yes
Minimizes number of swaps: Only n-1 swaps needed

Quick Sort

Time Complexity: O(n log n) average
Space Complexity: O(log n)

Quick Sort is a highly efficient divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm. It works by selecting a 'pivot' element and partitioning the array around the pivot.

How it works:
1. Choose a pivot element from the array
2. Partition: reorder array so elements smaller than pivot come before it, larger elements come after
3. Recursively apply above steps to sub-arrays

Best Case: O(n log n)
Worst Case: O(n²) - when pivot is always smallest or largest element
Average Case: O(n log n)

Stable: No (typical implementation)
In-place: Yes
Very fast in practice: One of the fastest sorting algorithms for average case

Merge Sort

Time Complexity: O(n log n)
Space Complexity: O(n)

Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that divides the input array into two halves, recursively sorts them, and then merges the two sorted halves.

How it works:
1. Divide array into two halves
2. Recursively sort both halves
3. Merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array

Merging process:
- Compare elements from both halves
- Place smaller element in result array
- Continue until all elements are merged

Best Case: O(n log n)
Worst Case: O(n log n)
Average Case: O(n log n)

Stable: Yes
In-place: No (requires extra space)
Guaranteed O(n log n): Unlike QuickSort, always performs well

Heap Sort

Time Complexity: O(n log n)
Space Complexity: O(1)

Heap Sort is a comparison-based sorting algorithm that uses a binary heap data structure. It divides input into sorted and unsorted regions, and iteratively shrinks the unsorted region by extracting the largest element.

How it works:
1. Build a max heap from input data
2. Swap root (maximum) with last element
3. Reduce heap size by 1
4. Heapify the root
5. Repeat steps 2-4 until heap size is 1

Heap property:
- Max Heap: Parent ≥ Children
- Tree is complete binary tree

Best Case: O(n log n)
Worst Case: O(n log n)
Average Case: O(n log n)

Stable: No
In-place: Yes
Guaranteed O(n log n) with O(1) space
